facts.claim: "Wonderful Nothing" is track 4 on Glass Animals' fourth album, I Love You So F***ing Much, released 19 July 2024.
Shazam lists the track as released 19 July 2024 by Polydor Records on I Love You So F***ing Much.
Dave Bayley is credited as the album's writer and sole producer. He also has credits for several instruments, programming, engineering and string arrangement.

Discogs credits for the album: mixed by Manny Marroquin, mastered by Chris Gehringer, engineered by Drew MacFarlane, Edmund Irwin-Singer and Matt Wiggins. Bayley is credited as writer, producer and engineer.

Album personnel include Bayley (vocals, drums, guitar, keyboards, synths, programming), Drew MacFarlane (keyboards, guitar), Edmund Irwin-Singer (bass, keyboards, synths) and Joe Seaward (drums, percussion). Leos Strings played strings.
Bayley says the track is "a song about love vs hate". It describes loving someone while intensely hating parts of them.
In April 2023 Bayley was in Los Angeles for writing sessions when a positive COVID test left him stranded in a hilltop rental. He wrote the entire album alone in those two weeks.
After writing the demos, Bayley took the songs back to his London studio and worked in a more structured way.
Matt Wiggins, who engineered the band's debut Zaba and mixed How to Be a Human Being, was brought in for the album's retro side. Drums were recorded in a live room with a window.
Mura Masa remixed the song as "Wonderful Nothing (Do Ya Thing Tiger Mix)", a bass-heavy dancefloor version. Its visualiser features the cow character from the "Show Pony" video.
Glass Animals formed in Oxford in 2010. Bayley, Joe Seaward, Ed Irwin-Singer and Drew MacFarlane are childhood friends. Bayley is the songwriter and producer.

research.lineage: Sits in the British psychedelic and indie-pop tradition of Glass Animals, with a retro-futuristic, 80s-flavoured synth-pop sound, and is described by Rolling Stone UK as a post-mortem of the band's 'Heat Waves' era.

draft:
The last thing **Wonderful Nothing** says is the only thing it means without a sneer: "There's the rub, maybe I'm the fool / I'm trying to stop, but I still love you." Everything before that couplet is a roast, and a vicious, very funny one. The narrator mocks someone's tired party, their tiger costume, their table manners. Then comes a mock shopping list from the mini-mart: the bitter truth, a better mood, a point of view to replace the old one, because "Yours went off in June 1992." It's the voice of someone who has rehearsed every insult in the shower and finally gets to use them all.

Dave Bayley has called it "a song about love vs hate," about loving someone while hating parts of them with real force. The lyric keeps both feelings in the room and never lets either one win. The contempt is loud, but the cracks show early. Midway through, the tone drops and the narrator admits to hoping and praying it would all change one day. The fight gets described as a gunfight where the other person drew blood and the narrator set themselves on fire. The cruelty works as armor, and the armor keeps slipping. In the refrains the requests turn inward: to be buried alive, to be put in a dungeon, just to make it out alive. Someone who wants to be punished this much is not over anything.

The music refuses to match the bile, and that gap is the song's best trick. Sustained synth pad chords lay a smooth floor. A synth bass repeats a simple line, a kick drum sets a steady, driving pulse at a moderate tempo, and a higher synth lead threads a melody over the top. The arrangement builds by stacking layers rather than lurching. The production is clean and polished, with reverb opening up space around everything. Bayley sings in a clear, slightly breathy tone. His delivery is melodic and almost sweet, which makes lines about pile-driving someone land like a smile with a knife behind it.

That retro-futurist, 80s-tinted synth-pop sits squarely in the band's British psychedelic indie-pop lineage. Rolling Stone UK read the song as a post-mortem of the band's "Heat Waves" era. Bayley wrote the album alone over two weeks in April 2023, stuck with COVID in a hilltop rental in Los Angeles. He later finished it in his London studio as its sole producer. The solitude shows. This is a song of one person arguing with someone who isn't there, winning every point, and losing anyway.

You come for the insults and stay for that last line, the moment a voice that's been laughing the whole time admits it can't stop caring.
